title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Data

state_abbr <- "TX"
geo_level <- "county"
year_acs <- 2024
survey <- "acs5"

# Median household income, people below poverty, and the poverty universe.
my_vars <- c(
  income = "B19013_001",
  pov = "B17001_002",
  povden = "B17001_001"
)

acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = geo_level,
  variables = my_vars,
  state = state_abbr,
  year = year_acs,
  survey = survey,
  geometry = TRUE,
  output = "wide"
) |>
  mutate(
    pov_rate = povE / povdenE,
    pov_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM),
    pov_ci_low = pmax(0, pov_rate - pov_moe),
    pov_ci_high = pmin(1, pov_rate + pov_moe)
  )

write_csv(st_drop_geometry(acs_wide), "acs_TX_2024.csv")

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Map: median household income

ggplot(acs_wide) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = NA) +

    labels = scales::dollar
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by Texas county",
    subtitle = "2024 ACS 5-year estimates",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey, via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Poverty-rate table
The table reports the ten counties with the highest and lowest estimated poverty rates. The MOE is the 90% confidence-interval half-width calculated with moe_prop().

county_rates <- acs_wide |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  transmute(County = NAME, pov_rate, pov_moe, ci_low = pov_ci_low, ci_high = pov_ci_high)

top10 <- county_rates |>
  arrange(desc(pov_rate)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

bottom10 <- county_rates |>
  arrange(pov_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

top10 |>
  transmute(
    County,
    `Poverty rate` = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `MOE (90% CI half-width)` = scales::percent(pov_moe, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Uncertainty check

# This finds the first adjacent pair in the high-poverty table with overlapping 90% confidence intervals.
overlap_pair <- top10 |>
  mutate(
    next_county = lead(County),
    next_low = lead(ci_low),
    next_high = lead(ci_high),
    overlaps = ci_low <= next_high & next_low <= ci_high
  ) |>
  filter(overlaps) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

overlap_pair |>
  transmute(
    County,
    `Poverty rate` = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `MOE (90% CI half-width)` = scales::percent(pov_moe, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Overlaps with` = next_county
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "An overlapping pair, if one occurs among the ten highest rates")

Dimmit County and Zapata County have overlapping 90% confidence intervals for their estimated poverty rates. Therefore, their apparent order in the ranking should not be treated as a precise difference: sampling uncertainty means either county could plausibly have the higher underlying poverty rate.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Methods note
I used 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for Texas counties. I identified these ACS variables using load_variables(2024, "acs5"). I mapped median household income (table B19013_001) and calculated the poverty rate as the number of people below poverty (B17001_002) divided by the poverty universe (B17001_001). Using a rate rather than a raw count avoids treating larger counties as more impoverished simply because they have more residents. I retained ACS margins of error and used moe_prop() to calculate the margin of error for the poverty rate. Dimmit County and Zapata County have overlapping 90% confidence intervals for their estimated poverty rates. Therefore, their apparent order in the ranking should not be treated as a precise difference: sampling uncertainty means either county could plausibly have the higher underlying poverty rate.

title: Research
text:
I am interested in how digital platforms shape the visibility of feminist content. One project I would like to develop examines how platform metrics, recommendation systems, and moderation practices affect the circulation of gender-related content on Chinese social media.
Data-generating process. A possible dataset for this project could combine records from my own content creation experience with publicly visible engagement metrics and documented moderation notices from platforms such as Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu. An important part of the research design would be to consider how platform interfaces, recommendation systems, and my own decisions about what to post shape the data that become observable.

Scraping five pages

urls <- paste0(
  "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-",
  1:5,
  ".html"
)

scrape_page <- function(page_url) {

  page <- read_html(page_url)

  books <- page |>
    html_elements("article.product_pod")

  titles <- books |>
    html_element("h3 a") |>
    html_attr("title")

  prices <- books |>
    html_element("p.price_color") |>
    html_text2()

  rating_classes <- books |>
    html_element("p.star-rating") |>
    html_attr("class")

  ratings <- sub("star-rating ", "", rating_classes)

  data.frame(
    title = titles,
    price = prices,
    rating = ratings
  )
}

pages <- lapply(urls, scrape_page)

books_5pages <- do.call(rbind, pages)

2. Wikipedia Foreign-Exchange Reserves

Scraping the table

wiki_url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_foreign-exchange_reserves"

wiki_page <- read_html(wiki_url)

wiki_tables <- wiki_page |>
  html_elements("table")

table3 <- wiki_tables[[3]] |>
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

names(table3) <- c(
  "country",
  "continent",
  "reserves_incl_gold",
  "change_incl_gold",
  "reserves_excl_gold",
  "change_excl_gold",
  "date",
  "ref"
)

reserves_raw <- table3[-c(1, 2), ]

reserves_clean <- reserves_raw |>

    continent,
    reserves_incl_gold,

  parse_number(reserves_clean$reserves_incl_gold)

reserves_clean$date <-

Changing the target table broke several assumptions from the first scraper. The foreign-exchange table was the third table on its page, contained eight columns, and included two header rows inside the extracted dataframe. In contrast, the population table was the first table, contained six columns, and its first row was a real World observation rather than an embedded header.
The date structure also changed. Most population observations reported a complete day-month-year date, but 10 observations reported only a year. I preserved this difference in precision rather than assigning an artificial month or day to year-only observations.

title: Assignment 4: Webscraping 1
text:
3. World Bank WDI Comparison

Fetching the same quantity from the World Bank

wdi_reserves <- WDI::WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = "FI.RES.TOTL.CD",
  start = 2024,
  end = 2026
)

wdi_latest <- wdi_reserves |>
  filter(!is.na(FI.RES.TOTL.CD)) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    reserves_million_usd = FI.RES.TOTL.CD / 1e6
  )

The WDI indicator is reported in current US dollars, while the Wikipedia table reports reserves in US$ millions. I therefore divided the WDI values by one million so that the two sources use the same unit.

real_countries <- WDI::WDI_data$country |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates") |>
  select(iso3c)

wdi_countries <- wdi_latest |>
  semi_join(real_countries, by = "iso3c")

World Bank regional and other aggregate observations were removed so that the comparison only used country-level entities.


Matching country names

wiki_for_join <- reserves_clean |>
  mutate(
    country_wdi = trimws(sub("\\s*\\*$", "", country)),
    country_wdi = recode(
      country_wdi,
      "Russia" = "Russian Federation",
      "Hong Kong" = "Hong Kong SAR, China",

      "Palestine" = "West Bank and Gaza",
      "Democratic Republic of the Congo" = "Congo, Dem. Rep.",
      "Republic of the Congo" = "Congo, Rep.",
      "Syria" = "Syrian Arab Republic",
      "Federated States of Micronesia" = "Micronesia, Fed. Sts.",
      "Yemen" = "Yemen, Rep.",

        "St. Vincent and the Grenadines",

comparison <- wiki_for_join |>
  left_join(
    wdi_countries |>
      select(
        country_wdi = country,
        year,
        reserves_million_usd
      ),
    by = "country_wdi"
  )

Country names differed between Wikipedia and the World Bank, so several names had to be standardized before joining the two datasets. Some Wikipedia observations still had no recent WDI value and were excluded from the numerical comparison.


Comparing the two sources

matched_comparison <- comparison |>
  filter(!is.na(reserves_million_usd)) |>
  mutate(
    difference_million =
      reserves_incl_gold - reserves_million_usd,
    percent_difference =
      100 * difference_million / reserves_million_usd,
    wikipedia_year = year(date),
    same_vintage = wikipedia_year == year
  )

comparison_summary <- data.frame(
  measure = c(
    "Matched observations",
    "Different calendar year",
    "Same calendar year",
    "Missing Wikipedia date"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(matched_comparison),
    sum(matched_comparison$same_vintage == FALSE, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(matched_comparison$same_vintage == TRUE, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(is.na(matched_comparison$same_vintage))
  )
)

Wikipedia reports a country-specific last-reported date, while the WDI observations returned by this query were annual values from 2024 or 2025. Therefore, many differences between the two sources can be explained by different reporting vintages.
However, substantial differences remained even when both observations came from the same calendar year. For example, South Sudan, São Tomé and Príncipe, Gabon, North Macedonia, and the United States showed large differences. This suggests that reporting vintage alone does not explain all discrepancies; source definitions, reporting practices, and data quality may also contribute.


When is scraping the right tool?
Scraping is appropriate when useful data are available on a web page but no usable API or structured download exists. When a documented API or bulk dataset is available, I would generally prefer it because it provides a more stable and reproducible interface than relying on webpage structure.

title: Assignment 4: Webscraping 1
text:
4. Data Plan
My research interest is how generative AI affects students’ information-seeking and evaluation behavior. For a web-based data collection project, I would collect public YouTube videos and comments related to students’ use of generative AI for studying, information searching, and academic work. YouTube is a useful source because students and educators publicly discuss how they use tools such as ChatGPT, what kinds of information they rely on, and how they evaluate AI-generated information. I would focus on videos and comments explicitly related to studying, research, fact-checking, or academic use of generative AI rather than general AI content.
I would use the official YouTube Data API rather than scraping YouTube webpages. Before collecting data, I would review YouTube’s Terms of Service and API policies to make sure that the planned collection and storage are permitted. Because YouTube provides structured access to public information through an API, scraping the HTML pages would not be necessary for this project. The API is also preferable because its fields are documented and less dependent on the visual structure of webpages.
I would begin with a defined set of search terms, such as “ChatGPT studying,” “AI for research,” and “students using ChatGPT.” I would first retrieve a limited set of relevant video IDs and then collect metadata and available public comments for those videos. Because the YouTube Data API uses a quota system, I would avoid repeatedly making unnecessary search requests. I would save retrieved video IDs and raw data locally and reuse these cached files during later stages of the project.
At the pilot stage, I would keep the collection relatively small, with dozens of videos and potentially several thousand comments. I would collect the data in batches and record the date of collection, search terms, video IDs, and API parameters so that the process can be reproduced. Raw API data would be stored separately from cleaned analysis data.
Possible failures include changes to API fields, deleted or unavailable videos, disabled or deleted comments, and changes in search results over time. I would detect these problems by checking the number of returned records, expected variable names, missing values, and API error messages each time the script runs. I would also keep a small set of known video IDs as a validation sample so that unexpected changes in API output can be detected.

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends
text:
What I Observed
1. Time window changes interval
Google Trends changes the temporal resolution depending on the time window.

Past 5 years: monthly

Past year: weekly

2. 0–100 is not raw search volume
The unit is a normalized search-interest index from 0 to 100.

100 means peak relative interest.
0 does not necessarily mean literally zero searches.

3. Changing the comparison set changes the values
After removing “Election,” the values for Trump and Kamala Harris changed substantially, showing that Google Trends values are relative to the query rather than fixed search counts.

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends
text:
Website vs. R

Temporal resolution:
The website returned monthly observations, while the R pull returned weekly observations. I aligned the two series at the monthly level before comparing them.
Difference in values:
The two series were not identical. After alignment, the mean difference (R - Website) was -7.59 points, the median was -6, and the differences ranged from -27.75 to -2.
Direction of difference:
In this comparison, the aggregated R values were consistently lower than the website values.
Interpretation:
This does not necessarily mean that one method is wrong. The discrepancy may reflect differences in temporal resolution, sampling, rescaling, and pull timing.

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends
text:
Method Comparison

Reproducibility:
R is more reproducible because the query parameters and data-processing steps are recorded in code. The website requires the user to manually record the search settings. However, reproducibility of the procedure does not guarantee that Google Trends will always return exactly the same values.
Provenance:
In R, the search terms, geography, time window, category, and search type are documented directly in the code. For the website download, these settings need to be recorded separately.
Scale:
R is more efficient for running many terms, countries, or repeated queries. The website is easier for a small number of searches, but becomes more time-consuming when the number of queries increases.
Fragility:
The R method can fail because of rate limiting. During this assignment, I received a 429 “Too Many Requests” error after repeated requests. The website method is less convenient for automation and can also be affected by interface changes or manual errors.
Additional R output:
The R object also included geographic breakdowns, related topics, and related queries that were not included in the website time-series CSV.
Harris vs. Kamala Harris:
The results for “Harris” and “Kamala Harris” were very different. “Harris” is a broader and more ambiguous search term, while “Kamala Harris” more closely matches the intended concept. This shows that the choice of search term is part of the measurement process.
Repeated R pull:
I ran the same R query twice a few minutes apart, and the values were identical in my test. However, Google Trends data are sampled and rescaled, so identical results in one test do not guarantee that future pulls will always be identical.

title: Assignment 1: Website Design Note
text:
This website was built with RStudio and Quarto and is published through GitHub Pages. The initial structure came from the course workshop handout, which provided starter files and introduced the workflow from Quarto source files to a published website. The handout describes the process as two connected steps: building the site locally in RStudio and Quarto, then publishing the rendered docs/ folder through GitHub Pages.
When I first completed the workshop, I had no previous experience with RStudio, Quarto, or GitHub Pages. I uploaded the workshop materials to YouMind and used it to help me interpret the instructions and work through the setup step by step. At that stage, much of my work was mechanical. I followed the starter structure, copied and modified code, and focused mainly on making the website work. I could produce a working page before I fully understood why the different files were needed.
While revisiting the site for Assignment 1, I began to understand the underlying workflow more clearly. I learned that each .qmd file functions as a source document for an individual page, while _quarto.yml organizes the website as a whole, including navigation and formatting. Running quarto render converts the source material into HTML files in the docs/ folder, which GitHub Pages then serves as the public website. This helped me understand the difference between the source files I edit and the final website that users see.
I also began to see why Quarto and RStudio are useful beyond building a personal website. The same workflow can combine narrative text, code, data analysis, and visualizations in one reproducible document. This changed how I understood the purpose of the assignment. The website is not only a place to display my CV or research interests; it is also an introduction to a workflow that can later support research reports, data analysis, and academic projects.
For the visual design, I retained the cosmo theme from the starter template because it is simple, readable, and appropriate for an academic website. I kept the amount of custom CSS limited because my priority at this stage is clarity and structure rather than complex visual design. I organized the navigation around Home, Research, Assignments, and CV so that the site can continue to grow as I complete coursework and develop research projects.
AI tools were part of this learning process. I used YouMind during the initial workshop to interpret instructions, guide technical steps, troubleshoot problems, and help draft or revise content. Later, I used ChatGPT as a second-stage reviewer to compare the website with the assignment requirements, identify placeholder or inaccurate content, and help revise the final version. Through this process, I also learned that AI-generated content needs to be checked carefully, especially when it makes assumptions about personal experience or research activities.
